label: lem:antiderivatives_diff_constant
title: Two antiderivatives differ by a constant
statement: Let $a, b \in \mathbb{R}$ with $a \le b$, and let $f : \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}$. Suppose $F$ and $G$ are both antiderivatives of $f$ on $(a,b)$, and that both $F$ and $G$ are continuous on the closed interval $[a,b]$. Then the difference $F - G$ is constant on $[a,b]$: specifically, $(F - G)(x) = (F - G)(a)$ for all $x \in [a,b]$.
proof: By Lemma~\ref{lem:antideriv_diff_zero_deriv}, the difference $F - G$ has derivative zero at every point of $(a,b)$. The function $F - G$ is continuous on $[a,b]$ because both $F$ and $G$ are. Applying Lemma~\ref{lem:zero_deriv_constant} to $F - G$, we conclude that $(F - G)(x) = (F - G)(a)$ for all $x \in [a,b]$.
